frameworks.name: Death Wish Mechanic
frameworks.definition: A product feature allowing life insurance customers to record specific intentions (financial, experiential, emotional) for what happens after their death, serving dual purposes: emotional personalization of the policy and a calculation tool for determining appropriate coverage amounts.

frameworks.name: Tackling vs. Ducking the Negative
frameworks.definition: A brand strategy framework where a product's inherent negative (uncomfortable subject matter, slow service, minority status) is addressed head-on rather than avoided, converting the liability into a salient differentiator. Rory Sutherland cites Avis (We Try Harder), Guinness (Good Things Come to Those Who Wait), and Dead Happy (humor around death) as canonical examples.

claims.text: Eddy Edwards argues that traditional 20- to 25-year level term life insurance is structurally overpriced for early years because insurers front-load payments to cover uncertainty about the customer's health in years 10-25; Dead Happy's 10-year rolling policy, which resets annually if health is unchanged, removes that long-tail risk premium and makes the product materially cheaper for the customer.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards
claims.mechanism: By capping the term at 10 years and requiring annual health confirmation, the insurer is only pricing risk it can credibly estimate, removing the uncertainty premium that inflates 20-25 year policies.
bounded_by: Customers with significantly deteriorating health cannot reset and therefore lose the rolling benefit

claims.text: Eddy Edwards asserts that the average traditional life insurance policy in the UK lapses after approximately seven to nine years despite being sold as a 20-25 year product, meaning customers pay heavily front-loaded premiums and then cancel before the term completes, creating poor value relative to a shorter annual-reset product.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards
claims.mechanism: Life events (marriage, children, mortgage changes) prompt customers to cancel old policies and start new ones, so they never stay the full 20-25 year term.

numbers.axis: average duration customers hold a traditional life insurance policy before cancellation

bounded_by: Customers who set policies and never update them may hold longer; edge cases in highly stable life circumstances

claims.text: Eddy Edwards states that approximately 8.5 million people in the UK lack life insurance who arguably should have it, and that roughly 42% of UK mortgage holders do not have life insurance, representing a large protection gap that Dead Happy is targeting.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards

numbers.axis: UK population without life insurance who likely need it

anchors.region: total uninsured who should be insured

claims.text: Eddy Edwards argues that cutting out brokers and independent financial advisers (IFAs) and selling directly to consumers online reduces customer acquisition friction and cost, enabling Dead Happy to attract a younger demographic (primarily ages 25-45, sweet spot early 30s) that would not typically engage via traditional IFA-mediated life insurance channels.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards
claims.mechanism: Traditional IFA intermediaries impose process friction (paperwork, formal meetings, time delays) that deter younger consumers who have no existing IFA relationship; removing intermediaries and offering a mobile-first four-question sign-up reduces that friction.

numbers.axis: Dead Happy active customer age range

bounded_by: Older customers who are accustomed to IFA guidance or require complex advice may not self-serve; intermediaries are needed for regulated will products

claims.text: Eddy Edwards claims that Dead Happy's irreverent brand personality and humor-led positioning is not merely cosmetic but serves a strategic function: by treating death as a topic worthy of humor and empowerment rather than avoidance, the brand builds an ongoing relationship with customers rather than a one-time transaction, differentiating it from conservative incumbents.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards
bounded_by: Brand tone may not suit traditional distribution through IFAs or corporate channels where conservative presentation is expected

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that when a product has an inherent negative attribute (such as a morbid subject matter or slow service), brands face a binary strategic choice: avoid the negative (duck it) or confront it directly (tackle it head on). Tackling head-on is typically the more creative and effective approach because it converts the liability into a salient, memorable differentiator, whereas avoidance leaves the problem unaddressed and the brand indistinct.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: brands with inherent product negatives or taboo subject matter
bounded_by: For products where the negative is severe enough to be genuinely disqualifying (e.g. safety failures), tackling it head-on may backfire by amplifying the negative beyond what humor or reframing can overcome

claims.text: Eddy Edwards asserts that Death Wishes (customer-specified instructions for how their life insurance payout is used) solve a known friction point in life insurance sales: most customers do not know how much coverage to buy. By walking customers through specific intended uses (mortgage coverage, funeral costs, experiential gifts), the Death Wish mechanic generates a more accurate and emotionally resonant coverage calculation, improving conversion and customer commitment.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards
claims.mechanism: Attaching a specific intended purpose to the payout makes the abstract concept of a lump sum concrete and personally meaningful, resolving both the cognitive barrier (how much?) and the emotional barrier (why bother?) simultaneously.
bounded_by: Death Wishes at the time of recording were not legally binding; legal enforceability requires integration with a will product

claims.text: Eddy Edwards argues that the life insurance industry's practice of isolating customers for 10-15 years between meaningful touchpoints after policy initiation creates a persistent trust deficit; incumbents only re-engage when they detect a life event (marriage, children, house move) and then typically use it to upsell a new more expensive policy rather than adjust the existing one.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards

numbers.axis: time between meaningful customer touchpoints in traditional life insurance

claims.text: Eddy Edwards contends that the conventional financial services and life insurance industry has created a psychological barrier by making policy updates (e.g., adding a one-off pension top-up) unnecessarily complex, requiring paper forms, posted checks, and multi-week waits with no confirmation of receipt; this friction is a lost revenue opportunity and a trust depressant that Dead Happy aims to eliminate via real-time digital dashboards.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland

claims.text: Eddy Edwards argues that life insurance, as a product selling against a future-death risk, is essentially the business of selling risk assumption: the insurer's value is in taking on the customer's mortality risk in exchange for premiums. This means that simplifying the risk-taking mechanism (fewer qualification questions, shorter covered periods) is both a product innovation and a pricing lever, because the insurer charges less when it assumes less uncertainty.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards
claims.mechanism: Fewer underwriting questions and a shorter term reduce the insurer's uncertainty about the risk profile, which reduces the risk premium embedded in pricing; the customer receives a cheaper product and the insurer maintains acceptable margins on a more predictable risk pool.
bounded_by: High-risk individuals who might disclose adverse health conditions cannot benefit from the simplified underwriting; the product is only viable for standard or low-risk health profiles

claims.text: Eddy Edwards states that Dead Happy's primary traffic channels at time of recording are Facebook, Instagram, and direct-response TV, with TV recently added; the brand is not relying on IFA referrals. This direct-to-consumer paid social and TV approach is responsible for attracting a younger, non-homeowner demographic that has not been targeted historically by life insurance brands.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards

claims.text: Eddy Edwards argues that the broader long-term vision for Dead Happy is not life insurance specifically but rather a comprehensive death services platform: covering wills, digital identity management, and any product or decision relevant to what a person wants to happen when they die, with life insurance serving as the initial proven product in this category.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards
bounded_by: Expansion into legally binding products (wills, power of attorney) introduces regulatory complexity that may constrain the irreverent brand tone

claims.text: Eddy Edwards asserts that the traditional life insurance sign-up process involves high perceived friction (IFA meetings, reams of paperwork, solicitors) that deters consumers from purchasing, even when they recognize the need. Dead Happy's four-question mobile sign-up eliminates this barrier and is a primary driver of conversion for consumers who would not otherwise initiate a policy.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards
claims.mechanism: Reducing the sign-up process from a multi-step IFA-mediated form-heavy process to four questions solvable on a mobile phone removes the primary activation friction, which is perceived effort cost rather than price or product relevance.
bounded_by: Customers who need complex coverage (high value, business insurance, complex beneficiaries) may require more underwriting than a four-question process can support

claims.text: Rory Sutherland observes that conventional financial institutions consistently fail to proactively cross-sell and upsell existing customers, citing David Ogilvy's 1970s observation that pension providers never contact customers to suggest adding contributions. Sutherland argues this persistent failure is a structural gap that digitally native, relationship-oriented brands like Dead Happy are positioned to exploit.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland

claims.text: Eddy Edwards contends that sharing death wishes (personal instructions about what should happen after death) publicly via social channels or privately with named beneficiaries via email or WhatsApp is a deliberate viral and trust mechanism: it normalizes the topic of death planning in social contexts, generates organic awareness for Dead Happy, and ensures the named beneficiary actually knows the policy exists and what the intentions are.
claims.speaker: Eddy Edwards
conditions: life insurance with Death Wish feature
claims.mechanism: Shareable death wishes create inherently social content (humorous wishes spread virally), solve the practical problem of beneficiary awareness, and reframe life insurance from a private administrative act into a social and relational one.
bounded_by: Legally binding instructions require integration with a will, which Dead Happy is developing but had not fully launched at time of recording

examples.text: Rory Sutherland illustrates the Tackling vs. Ducking the Negative framework with three canonical cases: Avis, ranked number two in car rental, addressed its inferiority by leaning into it with the campaign 'We're number two, so we try harder.' Guinness, whose slow pour is a product liability, converted it into a virtue with 'Good things come to those who wait.' American Express, which was less widely accepted than Visa or MasterCard, turned that into a status signal with 'The American Express card is not for everyone.' In each case, the brand's core problem became the brand's core message.

Eddy Edwards describes a real Death Wish example that circulated on Twitter: a man whose dying wish was that everyone assume he led a double life. At his funeral, the cortege was followed by three blacked-out Land Rovers, and actors in trench coats observed from a distance through binoculars. In reality, he was a bank manager at TSB. His widow honored the wish without revealing the truth, letting the mystery linger. Edwards uses this as an illustration of how Death Wishes can create emotional legacy and playful meaning, not just functional financial instructions.

Eddy Edwards recounts that when he was 22 or 23, an IFA visited his workplace to pitch pension plans with charts about compound growth and the importance of starting early. He pushed it away because it felt irrelevant to his life stage, too abstract, and too remote from his immediate concerns. He uses this personal example to argue that financial products delivered in a way that does not feel part of the customer's world will be rejected regardless of rational merit, validating Dead Happy's approach of making financial products feel emotionally relevant and convenient.

Rory Sutherland describes his ongoing paranoia about life insurance: he worries that if he dies, his wife will not know the policy exists, the insurance company will not proactively contact her, and the money will simply be kept. He also describes the experience of trying to make a one-off pension top-up payment as requiring writing a check, mailing it to an industrial estate in Bristol, and receiving no confirmation that it was received. He describes a Cambridge economist friend who also cannot make sense of the annual pension statement. These anecdotes illustrate the trust deficit and friction that characterize traditional financial services.

practices.text: Design life insurance or any long-term financial product with annual touchpoints and a customer-facing dashboard that allows real-time self-service updates to beneficiaries, coverage amounts, and personal wishes, rather than relying on infrequent IFA-mediated reviews.

When entering a taboo or uncomfortable category, explicitly lean into the discomfort in brand voice and naming rather than sanitizing it; humor and irreverence used authentically can transform a liability (death, aging, debt) into a point of differentiation and emotional connection.

For direct-to-consumer financial products, eliminate intermediaries and reduce sign-up steps to the minimum needed for regulatory compliance; measure acquisition channel mix with Facebook and Instagram as primary for younger demographics, supplemented by direct-response TV as the brand scales.

Design upsell and cross-sell paths into the core product flow (near-death insurance as a bolt-on, wills as the next product) from the outset, treating the initial product as the first relationship touchpoint rather than a standalone transaction.
